content: 1. In most cases, treatment duration is approximately two weeks. Obtain a urine nucleic acid amplification test to detect Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. 2. For uncomplicated infections with a risk of antibiotic-resistant pathogens: Preferred regimen: Ertapenem 1 g intravenously (IV) once daily (QD). Alternative regimens: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV QD, Imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours, or Tigecycline 100 mg IV as a single dose followed by 50 mg IV every 12 hours. 3. For complicated infections: Preferred regimen: Ertapenem 1 g IV QD. Alternative regimens: Cefepime 2 g IV every 12 hours, Imipenem 500 mg IV every 6 hours, or Tigecycline 100 mg IV as a single dose followed by 50 mg IV every 12 hours. 4. For infections complicated by bacteremia or suspected prostatic abscess: Preferred regimens: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours or Levofloxacin 500 mg IV every 24 hours. Alternative regimens: Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 hours combined with Levofloxacin 500–750 mg orally (PO) QD, Ertapenem 1 g IV every 24 hours, or Piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV every 6 hours. Note: Treat for four weeks. Obtain blood cultures, consider genitourinary imaging, and switch from IV to oral therapy once blood cultures are sterile and abscesses are drained. 5. For chronic bacterial prostatitis: Preferred regimens: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 12 hours or Levofloxacin 500 mg IV every 24 hours. Alternative regimen: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) double-strength (DS) tablet twice daily (BID). 6. For pyelonephritis: Condition 1: Patients not requiring hospitalization where community uropathogen resistance to fluoroquinolones is ≤10%. Preferred regimen: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally BID for 7 days ± an initial 400-mg IV dose of Ciprofloxacin. Alternative regimen: A once-daily oral fluoroquinolone, such as Ciprofloxacin 1000 mg extended-release for 7 days or Levofloxacin 750 mg for 5 days. Note: If fluoroquinolone resistance exceeds 10%, an initial IV dose of a long-acting antimicrobial (e.g., Ceftriaxone 1 g or a consolidated 24-hour dose of an aminoglycoside) is recommended. Condition 2: When the uropathogen is known to be susceptible. Preferred regimen: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg (1 double-strength tablet) BID orally for 14 days. Note: If susceptibility is unknown, an initial IV dose of a long-acting antimicrobial (e.g., Ceftriaxone 1 g or a consolidated 24-hour dose of an aminoglycoside) is recommended. Condition 3: Patients requiring hospitalization (e.g., high fever, leukocytosis, vomiting, dehydration, or sepsis). Preferred regimen: IV antimicrobial therapy, such as a fluoroquinolone, an aminoglycoside ± ampicillin, an extended-spectrum cephalosporin or penicillin ± an aminoglycoside, or a carbapenem. Note: The choice of agent should be guided by local resistance data and tailored based on susceptibility results. 7. For sterile pyuria: Definition: Pyuria is defined as ≥10 white blood cells (WBCs) per cubic millimeter in a urine specimen, ≥3 WBCs per high-power field in unspun urine, a positive Gram stain of unspun urine, or a positive leukocyte esterase test on a urinary dipstick. Sterile pyuria refers to persistent WBCs in urine without bacterial growth on aerobic culture. Causes: Infectious etiologies: gynecologic infections, urethritis (e.g., Chlamydia, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma), prostatitis, balanitis, appendicitis, viral infections, genitourinary tuberculosis, fungal infections, parasitic diseases (e.g., trichomoniasis, schistosomiasis). Non-infectious etiologies: recent antibiotic use, recent urinary tract infection, urinary catheters, recent cystoscopy, urinary stones, foreign bodies (e.g., surgical mesh, retained stents), urinary tract neoplasms, pelvic irradiation, urinary fistulas, polycystic kidney disease, renal transplant rejection, renal vein thrombosis, interstitial nephritis, papillary necrosis, interstitial cystitis, inflammatory diseases (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, Kawasaki disease). 8. Pathogen-directed antimicrobial therapy: Tuberculosis: Isoniazid, Rifampin, Ethambutol, and Pyrazinamide for 3–6 months. Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly (IM) in a single dose, followed by Azithromycin 1 g PO in a single dose or Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 7 days. Chlamydia: Azithromycin 1 g PO in a single dose or Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 7 days. Alternative: Erythromycin base 500 mg PO four times daily (QID) for 7 days. Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma: Azithromycin, Levofloxacin, or Moxifloxacin. Genital herpes: Acyclovir 400 mg PO three times daily (TID) for 7–10 days, Acyclovir 200 mg PO five times daily for 7–10 days, Famciclovir 250 mg PO TID for 7–10 days, or Valacyclovir 1 g PO BID for 7 days. Trichomoniasis: Metronidazole 2 g PO in a single dose or Tinidazole 2 g PO in a single dose. Fungal infections: Fluconazole, Posaconazole, Echinocandins, or Amphotericin B. Schistosomiasis: Praziquantel 20 mg/kg PO BID for 1–2 days. 9. For syphilis (Treponema pallidum): Primary and secondary syphilis: Adults: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units (MU) IM in a single dose. Pediatrics: Benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg (up to 2.4 MU) IM in a single dose. Latent syphilis: Early latent syphilis: Same as primary/secondary syphilis. Late latent syphilis or unknown duration: Adults: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM for 3 doses at 1-week intervals. Pediatrics: Benzathine penicillin G 50,000 units/kg (up to 2.4 MU) IM for 3 doses at 1-week intervals. Tertiary syphilis: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM for 3 doses at 1-week intervals. Neurosyphilis: Preferred: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 3–4 MU IV every 4 hours or continuously for 10–14 days. Alternative: Procaine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM daily for 10–14 days combined with Probenecid 500 mg PO QID for 10–14 days.
